about: "Make it specific" prompts for Unit 4 (docs/apmacro-architecture.md, "Make it specific"): a free-response task the readers often score as too vague, a checklist, an answer that earns the point and one that misses it, and a builder (slots) that assembles the specific answer. Every number is recomputed in JUSTIFY_NUMBERS (scripts/lib/apmacro-exams.mjs).

prompts.title: Bond prices when interest rates rise
prompts.prompt: Talia owns a bond that pays 3% a year. New bonds now pay 5%. Explain what happens to the price of Talia's bond.
checklist: Says new bonds pay more, so buyers prefer them
Says Talia's bond must sell at a lower price to attract a buyer
States the rule: bond prices and interest rates move in opposite directions

earns.answer: Buyers can now get 5% on a new bond, so no one will pay full price for a bond paying 3%. Talia's bond has to sell at a lower price, so its price falls. Bond prices and interest rates move in opposite directions.
earns.why: It explains the mechanism with the two rates and states the inverse relationship.

misses.answer: Her bond is worth more because interest rates are higher now.
misses.why: A higher market rate makes an old, lower-paying bond less attractive, so its price falls.

why.1: The new bonds pay more each year for the same price.
It pays less than new bonds, so it must cost less.
why.2: Its fixed payment is worth less when new bonds pay more.

prompts.title: Expected and actual real interest rates
prompts.prompt: Ressa's bank lends at a nominal interest rate of 8%, expecting inflation of 3%. Inflation turns out to be 6%. Calculate the real rate the bank expected and the real rate it earned, and explain who gains.
checklist: Expected real rate = 8% - 3% = 5%
Real rate earned = 8% - 6% = 2%
Says the borrower gains and the bank loses from the surprise inflation

earns.answer: The bank expected a real interest rate of 8% - 3% = 5%. With actual inflation of 6%, it earned 8% - 6% = 2%. The unexpected inflation moves buying power to the borrower, who gains, while the bank loses.
earns.why: Both real rates are computed from the right inflation figure, and the winner is named.

misses.answer: The real rate the bank earns is 8% + 6% = 14% for the year.
misses.why: The real rate subtracts inflation from the nominal rate; adding it goes the wrong way.

why.1: That adds expected inflation.
why.2: That uses the actual inflation, not the expected.

why.1: That is the rate the bank expected; inflation came in higher.

prompts.title: The three functions of money
prompts.prompt: Identify the function of money in each case and explain one: (1) a menu lists every meal's price in dollars; (2) Kim pays for groceries with her debit card; (3) Sam keeps \$300 in his checking account for a trip next month.
checklist: (1) unit of account: prices are measured in money
(2) medium of exchange: money is accepted in trade
(3) store of value: money holds buying power until later

earns.answer: (1) The menu uses money as a unit of account, a common measure of value. (2) Paying for groceries uses money as a medium of exchange. (3) Keeping \$300 for next month uses money as a store of value: it holds buying power over time, without having to find a buyer for some other good later.
earns.why: Each case gets the right function, and the explanation says what the function does.

misses.answer: All three are money being used to buy things.
misses.why: Only the second is a purchase; pricing and saving are the other two functions, and none is named.

why.1: Nothing is bought yet; the prices just measure value.
why.2: Nothing is being saved; the menu measures value.

why.1: Sam is not trading yet; he is holding value for later.

prompts.title: A new deposit and the money supply
prompts.prompt: Under limited reserves with a required reserve ratio of 0.1, Rafe deposits \$1,000 of cash in his checking account. Calculate the bank's new excess reserves and the largest possible change in the money supply from the bank lending them.
checklist: Required reserves: 1,000 x 0.1 = \$100; excess reserves: 1,000 - 100 = \$900
Money multiplier: 1 / 0.1 = 10
Largest change from lending: 900 x 10 = \$9,000

earns.answer: Required reserves on the deposit are 1,000 x 0.1 = \$100, so excess reserves are 1,000 - 100 = \$900. The money multiplier is 1 / 0.1 = 10, so lending the excess reserves can raise the money supply by at most 900 x 10 = \$9,000. The deposit itself does not change the money supply, since cash became a checkable deposit.
earns.why: It finds excess reserves first and multiplies those, not the whole deposit, with every step shown.

misses.answer: The money supply can rise by 1,000 x 10 = \$10,000.
misses.why: That multiplies the whole deposit; only the \$900 of excess reserves can be lent out.

why.1: \$100 is required reserves, which the bank must keep.
why.2: The bank must keep 10% of the deposit.

dm.label: Largest change in the money supply

why.1: That multiplies the whole deposit.
why.2: That counts the first loan alone.

prompts.title: A bond purchase on the money market graph
prompts.prompt: Danby's central bank, which works with limited reserves, buys government bonds. Explain the effect on a correctly labeled money market graph.
checklist: Labels the axes: nominal interest rate and quantity of money
Says buying bonds adds bank reserves, so the money supply (vertical) shifts right
Says the nominal interest rate falls from i1 to i2

earns.answer: On a money market graph (nominal interest rate on the vertical axis, quantity of money on the horizontal), buying bonds pays money into banks' reserves, so banks can lend more and the money supply rises: MS shifts right from MS1 to MS2. With money demand unchanged, the nominal interest rate falls from i1 to i2.
earns.why: Correct axes, the right curve and direction, and the new rate compared with the old.

misses.answer: The real interest rate falls because money demand shifts right.
misses.why: The money market uses the nominal rate, and the curve that moves is the money supply, not money demand.

why.1: The money market uses the nominal rate; the real rate is for loanable funds.
The central bank's purchase changes the quantity of money, not how much people want to hold.
why.2: Buying bonds adds money; selling would remove it.

prompts.title: A higher price level and money demand
prompts.prompt: The price level in Danby rises, and the central bank does not act. Explain the effect on the money market and the nominal interest rate.
checklist: Says people need more money for the same purchases, so money demand shifts right
Says the money supply does not move
Says the nominal interest rate rises

earns.answer: With a higher price level, people need more money to buy the same goods, so money demand shifts right from MD1 to MD2. The money supply does not move, so the nominal interest rate rises from i1 to i2.
earns.why: It names the curve that moves and why, and compares the new rate with the old.

misses.answer: The money supply falls, so the interest rate rises.
misses.why: Nothing changed the money supply; the higher price level raises money demand.

why.1: The central bank did not act, so the money supply is unchanged.
More demand for a fixed money supply raises its price, the interest rate.

prompts.title: The tool for a recession with ample reserves
prompts.prompt: Pellow's central bank operates with ample reserves, and the economy is in a recession. Identify the action the central bank would take and explain how it changes the policy rate.
checklist: Names lowering its administered rates, such as the interest rate on reserve balances
Says reserve supply is not changed to move the rate
Says the policy rate falls with the administered rate

earns.answer: With ample reserves, the central bank lowers its administered rates, chiefly the interest rate on reserve balances. Banks earn less for holding reserves, so the rate at which they lend reserves to each other, the policy rate, falls with it. The supply of reserves is not changed to move the rate.
earns.why: The tool matches the framework, and the link to the policy rate is explained.

misses.answer: The central bank buys bonds to increase the money supply.
misses.why: Buying bonds is the limited-reserves tool; with ample reserves the rate is moved by the administered rates.

tool.label: The tool
options: lower the interest rate on reserve balances

why.1: Open market operations set the rate in a limited-reserves framework.
why.2: Reserve requirements play no part with ample reserves.

why.1: A lower administered rate pulls the policy rate down.

prompts.title: The tool for inflation with limited reserves
prompts.prompt: Corra's central bank works with limited reserves, and the economy has an inflationary gap. Identify an open market operation it would use and explain its effect on the money supply and the nominal interest rate.
checklist: Names selling government bonds
Says buyers pay with money that leaves bank reserves, so the money supply falls
Says the nominal interest rate rises

earns.answer: The central bank sells government bonds. Buyers pay for them with money that leaves banks' reserves, so banks lend less and the money supply falls (MS shifts left). With money demand unchanged, the nominal interest rate rises, which lowers investment and AD to close the gap.
earns.why: The open market operation fits the gap, and its effect on reserves, the money supply and the rate is explained.

misses.answer: The central bank raises taxes to slow spending.
misses.why: Taxes are fiscal policy, set by the government, not a central bank tool.

why.1: Buying bonds adds reserves, which raises the money supply.
Money paid for the bonds leaves the banking system.

prompts.title: From a lower policy rate to real output
prompts.prompt: Pellow's central bank (above) lowers the interest rate on reserve balances. Explain how this affects real output and the price level in the short run, naming every link.
checklist: Says the policy rate falls, and other interest rates follow
Says lower rates raise investment and interest-sensitive consumption
Says AD shifts right, so real output and the price level rise

earns.answer: The lower administered rate lowers the policy rate, which lowers other interest rates in the economy. Cheaper borrowing raises investment and interest-sensitive consumption, which shifts AD right, so real output rises and the price level rises in the short run.
earns.why: Every link from the tool to output and prices is named in order.

misses.answer: Lower interest rates raise real output and the price level.
misses.why: The links between the rate and output, spending and AD, are missing.

why.1: Banks pass the lower policy rate on to borrowers.
Cheaper borrowing makes more projects worth doing.
Spending changed, so demand moves, not supply.

prompts.title: More saving in the loanable funds market
prompts.prompt: Households in Fenwick decide to save a larger share of their income. Explain the effect on a correctly labeled loanable funds graph.
checklist: Labels the axes: real interest rate and quantity of loanable funds
Says the supply of loanable funds shifts right
Says the real interest rate falls and the quantity of loanable funds rises

earns.answer: On the loanable funds graph (real interest rate on the vertical axis, quantity of loanable funds on the horizontal), more saving shifts the supply of loanable funds right, from SLF1 to SLF2. The real interest rate falls and the quantity of loanable funds borrowed and lent rises.
earns.why: Correct axes, the right curve and direction, and both outcomes compared with the start.

misses.answer: The nominal interest rate falls because the demand for loanable funds rises.
misses.why: Saving is the supply of loanable funds, and that market uses the real interest rate.

why.1: Savers supply loanable funds; borrowers demand them.
More funds to lend at each rate lower the rate.
